issues.title: When a Card Becomes a Joke: Two Lives of the Magic 'Meme Card'
issues.dek: Polygon's new ranking of Magic: The Gathering's funniest cards reveals that 'meme card' isn't one thing — it's two, and the difference matters.
editorial: Magic: The Gathering has a funny relationship with humor. Polygon's new ranked list of the game's ten funniest meme cards draws a line that most casual usage blurs: some cards were never meant to be funny but somehow became jokes among players, while newer cards often go out of their way to recreate viral memes and deeply silly pieces of pop culture [C-SRC-1].

Those are two different phenomena wearing the same label. On one side sit accidents — cards like Indestructible Aura, which dates all the way back to the Legends set in 1994 and which Polygon describes as feeling like it was designed specifically to become a meme, even though it's 'less an internet meme printed on a Magic card and more like a meme Magic accidentally created for itself' [C-SRC-1]. On the other side sit deliberate gestures: the Marvel Super Heroes set turning some of the strangest comic panels into official Magic art, and recent Secret Lair Drops embracing everything from SpongeBob memes to the bizarre corners of internet culture [C-SRC-1].

Even the deliberate category has texture. Polygon singles out Garfield's Counterspell as 'less of a recreation of one specific internet meme and more of a perfect translation of Garfield's entire comedic personality in Magic' — a third mode that references a comedic sensibility rather than any single image [C-SRC-1].

What we're flagging here is the vocabulary, not a verdict. 'Meme card' is doing real work in coverage like this, but the packets don't establish that players use the term consistently, or that it has one settled meaning. Accidental in-joke, licensed meme reference, and tonal homage all travel under the same word. If someone tells you a card is 'a meme,' it's worth asking which kind they mean.

As always: this describes observed usage in games media as of the source's publication date. It says nothing about any reader's identity or taste, and it doesn't claim the term means the same thing everywhere it appears.

issues.title: Beavers With Bagpipes: When a Trade War Gets an AI Anthem
issues.kicker: A viral music video shows how AI-made content can carry real political feeling — and why the label matters as much as the joke.
issues.dek: Velvet Signal culture desk, proposed edition. One signal, observed use, ambiguity kept intact.
editorial: The latest front in the US-Canada trade war, per Business Insider, isn't tariffs — it's an army of Mountie bears playing bagpipes. The AI-made music video "Canadian Resistance Army — Trade War" has gone viral as an expression of Canadian defiance toward US tariffs, and has been picked up as an unlikely patriotic anthem [C-SRC-2].

The production is openly synthetic. The video's YouTube page labels it "made with AI," and the creator demonflyingfox — who has 490,000 YouTube subscribers — says in the description that it used Kling AI for video generation, ElevenLabs for voice, Suno for music, and InVideo for editing [C-SRC-2].

What makes it worth your attention is the friction between those two facts. Felix Simon, a research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, said the video taps into a subject "that is on people's minds anyway" and reframes a serious conflict in a more digestible form [C-SRC-2]. In other words: audiences appear to be engaging with AI-generated content not despite its artificiality but as a format for processing a real geopolitical moment.

We're not declaring a universal meaning here. Whether viewers experience the video as satire, sincere patriotism, or something in between isn't established by the available reporting — and Business Insider notes it's not the first time AI-generated content has turned a political moment into a viral video [C-SRC-2]. What we can say is what was observed: an openly AI-labeled video, made with a disclosed toolchain, circulating as political expression.

issues.title: Velvet Signal — Wellbeing Edition
issues.dek: A quiet refresher on screens, naps, and how much sleep adults actually need — drawn from the NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
editorial: If your evenings have started to blur into your bedtime, this edition is a friendly checkpoint rather than a scolding. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) notes that artificial light from screens — phones, laptops, televisions — can signal the brain that it's time to be awake, and that this light exposure can translate into shorter sleep and irregular sleep schedules in both children and adults [W-SRC-1]. A study partly funded by NHLBI found that smartphone use before bed was associated with shorter sleep duration than normal and worse sleep quality during the night [W-SRC-1].

The practical suggestion from experts is modest and doable: power down devices at least 30 minutes before getting into bed [W-SRC-1]. Thirty minutes is not a moral test — it's a small buffer that gives your brain a chance to shift gears. Some people will find it easy; others, especially those whose evenings involve caregiving, shift work, or shared screens, will find it harder. Individual variation is real, and this guidance is general, not a prescription.

On naps, NHLBI's guidance is similarly gentle: a daytime nap may boost alertness and performance, adults should keep naps to no more than 20 minutes, and if you have trouble falling asleep at night, it may help to limit naps or take them earlier in the afternoon [W-SRC-2]. Napping is not a failure state — it's a tool, and the timing and length matter for how it interacts with your night.

Finally, the baseline: NHLBI, citing recommendations from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommends 7 to 9 hours of sleep per day for adults 18 and older, with different ranges for children and teens [W-SRC-5]. Over time, not getting enough quality sleep — what NHLBI calls sleep deficiency — can raise the risk of heart disease, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and stroke [W-SRC-5]. None of this replaces professional care: if sleep problems persist or distress you, a clinician is the right next stop.
This edition restates and independently re-confirms guidance published in earlier issues; the ledger below marks those confirmations explicitly.

issues.title: YOLO-Master's MoE era: pruning, LoRA, and a faster NMS dial
issues.dek: Tencent's YOLO-Master spent January and February 2026 turning its Mixture-of-Experts pipeline into something you can actually operate: diagnose it, prune it, fine-tune it with LoRA, and trade accuracy against speed at inference time.
editorial: The most operationally interesting change here is the pruning pair. YOLO-Master added two MoE tools on 2026/01/16: diagnose_model, which visualizes expert utilization and routing behavior to surface redundant experts, and prune_moe_model, which physically removes those redundant experts and reconstructs the routers for efficient inference without retraining [M-SRC-1]. That second half matters: pruning without a retraining pass turns expert cleanup from a research project into a maintenance task.

Speed-versus-accuracy got an explicit dial on 2026/01/09 with Cluster-Weighted NMS (CW-NMS), exposed as a cluster boolean flag described as cluster NMS (MoE optimized) for trading mAP against speed [M-SRC-1]. If you deploy across heterogeneous hardware, this is the kind of switch worth benchmarking per target rather than setting once.

Training-side changes landed in the same window. MoE loss was added explicitly to training on 2026/01/07, appearing as its own moe_loss column in the epoch log alongside box, cls, and dfl losses [M-SRC-1], and the MoE script was split into modules that same day [M-SRC-1]. On 2026/02/13 the project added LoRA support for model training and released version v2026.02 [M-SRC-1].

Deployment paths widened too: ncnn-YOLO-Master-android gained support for deploying YOLO-Master on 2026/01/14 [M-SRC-1], and TensorRT-YOLO was credited with accelerating YOLO-Master on 2026/01/07 [M-SRC-1].

Provenance note: the repository was transferred from Repo isLinXu to Tencent on 2026/01/16 [M-SRC-1]. The packet is a changelog snapshot rather than a release announcement, and its excerpt is truncated mid-list, so treat the v2026.02 tag as the only explicit version marker in this source.

issues.title: Movement, Sleep, and Downtime: Why the Full Combo Matters for Student Wellbeing
issues.dek: A systematic review of university students finds that the mental-health payoff of healthy routines is largest when physical activity, sleep, and sedentary-time recommendations are met together — and that adherence is uneven across students.
editorial: A systematic review examining physical activity and mental health in university students reports that adhering to recommendations for physical activity, sleep, and sedentary behavior was associated with lower distress and higher wellbeing — and that the greatest mental health benefit appeared when all three guideline areas were met at once (W-SRC-2).

The same review found that students with chronic conditions or disabilities (CCD) were less likely to meet the 24-hour movement guidelines, and that students with multimorbidities or developmental disabilities showed the lowest adherence rates (W-SRC-2). That's a useful corrective to any one-size-fits-all framing: the students who might benefit most from these routines may also face the steepest barriers to following them.

Methodologically, the review captured updated and postpandemic evidence, combining search terms for physical activity (such as physical activity, exercise, and sedentary) with mental-health terms (stress, anxiety, depression, wellbeing) filtered to college and university populations (W-SRC-2).

Two honest caveats. First, the findings described here are associations — the review reports that adherence was 'associated with' lower distress and higher wellbeing, not that the routines caused those outcomes (W-SRC-2). Second, our source excerpt is a fragment of the full paper; we can see the headline association and the adherence gaps clearly, but not the full strength-of-evidence assessment, so treat the details as needing fuller review before being treated as settled (W-SRC-2, needs-review).
This is general wellbeing information, not individualized medical advice. If sleep, movement, or stress feel like problems in your life, a healthcare professional is the right place to start.

issues.title: The raw side of the fridge
issues.dek: Leftovers get all the attention, but the countdown for most proteins starts before the stove is ever lit. This issue covers the raw-storage clock, a calmer way to thaw, and one freezer caveat worth knowing.
editorial: Most kitchen food-safety advice fixates on the after — the leftovers, the reheating, the mystery container pushed to the back. But the storage clock for meat, poultry, and fish starts at the grocery store, not the dinner table. Two USDA sources agree on the headline numbers: raw poultry and ground meats keep just 1 to 2 days in the refrigerator, a window short enough that the same-week plan matters [P-SRC-1, P-SRC-4].

Whole cuts get more breathing room. Other red meats — think steaks and roasts rather than ground or minced — keep 3 to 5 days refrigerated [P-SRC-4]. That difference is structural: grinding and processing spread any surface bacteria throughout, which is why the ground versions run on the shorter clock.

Once those raw days are spent and the food is cooked, the thaw matters too. The take-out guidance recommends thawing wrapped, cooked meat or poultry on a tray in the refrigerator, allowing about 24 hours for every 5 pounds — small packages of stuffing, gravy, or potatoes thaw faster and can go into the fridge later [P-SRC-5]. And if plans change, frozen food can go directly into the oven without thawing at all [P-SRC-5].
One freezer footnote: salads made with mayonnaise do not freeze well [P-SRC-5]. The refrigerator is their home; the freezer will only change their texture for the worse.

A note on limits, because it matters: these windows describe how long food keeps at proper refrigerator and freezer temperatures. They cannot tell you whether a specific container is safe when the timeline, the temperature, or the storage history is unknown. The guidance is blunt on that point — when in doubt, throw it out, and don't taste to check [P-SRC-5].

issues.title: wellbeing-011
issues.dek: NHLBI's sleep guidance puts numbers on 'enough' — and explains why those hours do quiet, essential work while you're unconscious.
editorial: Sleep advice often stops at 'get more of it,' which is about as useful as being told to 'eat better.' This week's update comes from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), which does something more helpful: it publishes age-by-age ranges for how much sleep people need each day — 7 to 9 hours for adults 18 and older, with different ranges for babies, children, and teens [W-SRC-5].

Those ranges matter because sleep isn't downtime. NHLBI describes it as the period when your heart and blood vessels heal and repair themselves — and warns that over time, not getting enough quality sleep (what it calls sleep deficiency) can raise the risk of heart disease, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and stroke [W-SRC-5].

The 'why' runs deeper still. Your body runs on internal clocks with cycles of roughly 24 hours, regulated by light, darkness, and your sleep schedule; once asleep, you cycle through sleep stages in a predictable pattern [W-SRC-4]. Skimp on sleep — or on sleep quality — and NHLBI says the effects reach your heart, your respiratory system, your metabolism, and your ability to think clearly and focus [W-SRC-4].

One honest caveat: these are population-level ranges, not a prescription. Where you land within 7 to 9 hours — or whether a persistent sleep problem deserves a clinician's attention — is individual. NHLBI's materials are general guidance, not a substitute for professional care.

If you take one practical step from this issue, make it the one NHLBI keeps returning to: give yourself enough time to sleep in the first place. It's often the first thing busy people squeeze out — and the easiest to protect once you treat it as non-negotiable [W-SRC-1].

issues.title: Two Sleep Budgets: Feeling Awake vs. Being Healthy
issues.dek: NHLBI draws a quiet but useful line between the sleep you need to feel alert and the sleep you need to stay well — and the gap between them is exactly where individual variation lives.
editorial: It is tempting to treat sleep as a single number: hours in, alertness out. But the NHLBI's Sleep Brochure makes a distinction worth sitting with — there is a difference between the sleep needed to feel awake and the sleep needed to be healthy, and the brochure describes that difference alongside practical tips for getting a good night's sleep. [W-SRC-5]

Why does the distinction matter? Because 'I function fine on little sleep' and 'this amount of sleep supports my health' can be two different questions. Feeling awake is a short-term signal; health is a longer ledger. The brochure's framing leaves room for the fact that people vary — the amount that keeps one person sharp is not automatically the amount that keeps another person well. [W-SRC-5]

For readers who want to go deeper, NHLBI's patient booklet 'Your Guide to Healthy Sleep' offers science-based information about the types of sleep, common sleep myths, and practical tips for getting adequate sleep and coping with jet lag and nighttime shift work. It also covers avoiding dangerous drowsy driving and gives an overview of certain sleep disorders, including insomnia, sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, narcolepsy, and some parasomnias. [W-SRC-2] A Spanish-language, easy-to-read fact sheet, 'En resumen: su guía para un sueño saludable,' summarizes the critical messages of the English guide and includes information on sleep and driving; it was updated in 2013. [W-SRC-1]

One practical starting point, if the distinction above prompts a personal audit: NHLBI advises making sure you give yourself enough time to sleep. With enough sleep each night, people may find they are happier and more productive during the day — and making time to sleep helps protect health and well-being now and in the future. [W-SRC-3]

A note on scope: this is general public-health guidance, not a diagnosis or a prescription. Sleep needs differ from person to person, and persistent sleep problems — the booklet names several common disorders — are a conversation for a qualified clinician, not a newsletter. [W-SRC-2]

issues.title: Velvet Signal — Proposed Edition & Claim Ledger
issues.dek: The cold cuts, the ham, the tubs of salad: a shelf-by-shelf guide to the foods that never announce their age.
editorial: You have probably internalized the leftover clock by now — three to four days in the fridge, and you have heard it from us before. But the refrigerator holds a quieter cast of characters: the half-eaten ham, the deli turkey in its crinkling sleeve, the tub of macaroni salad from the corner deli. None of them come with a countdown timer, and all of them have one. This week we transcribe the clock for the packaged and prepared foods — so the second shelf stops being a guessing game.

Start with the deli drawer. Luncheon meats and vacuum-packed sliced meats keep two weeks unopened, but once the seal breaks, the window collapses to three to five days. Hot dogs follow the same pattern with a steeper drop: two weeks sealed, one week once the package is open. The pattern is worth noticing — opening a package is the moment the clock speeds up, so label the day you opened it. [P-SRC-1] [P-SRC-5]

Ham deserves its own line, because the answer depends on the cut. A fully cooked whole ham keeps seven days; a half, three to five; slices, three to four. All of them hold one to two months in the freezer if you will not get through them in time. [P-SRC-1] [P-SRC-5]

The prepared-foods case runs on its own schedule. Store-made or homemade egg, chicken, tuna, ham, and macaroni salads keep three to five days. Store-cooked dinners and entrées keep three to four. The one genuinely urgent item: anything pre-stuffed — pork chops, lamb chops, chicken breasts — gets a single day in the refrigerator, and pre-stuffed chops do not freeze well. If stuffing is the plan, stuff the day you cook. [P-SRC-1] [P-SRC-5]

Two pantry-adjacent notes. Bacon keeps seven days refrigerated or a month frozen. Commercial mayonnaise labeled "refrigerate after opening" keeps two months in the fridge — and should not be frozen at all. [P-SRC-5] And a standing habit worth keeping: once a week, walk the fridge and discard whatever perishable food should no longer be eaten. The general rule of thumb still holds — about four days for cooked leftovers, one to two for raw poultry and ground meats. [P-SRC-1] When in doubt about a specific item, the guidance is blunt: foods stored too long may spoil or become unsafe, and you should not taste them to find out. [P-SRC-3] We will not tell you whether the specific container in your fridge is safe — no chart can, without knowing its full history of time and temperature. issues.title: A Sleep-Hygiene Tune-Up: Screens, Naps, and Giving Sleep Its Time Back
issues.dek: NHLBI's sleep guidance points to two small, adjustable habits — when the screens go dark and how long the afternoon nap runs — that shape how the night goes.
editorial: Sleep hygiene sounds clinical, but the idea behind it is simple: the environment you've built and the habits you've kept around bedtime quietly set the terms for the night. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute suggests periodically taking stock of both — and a good place to start, they say, is the screens [W-SRC-3].

Artificial light from phones, laptops, and televisions can signal the brain that it's time to be awake. That exposure can translate into lost sleep and irregular schedules, in children and adults alike [W-SRC-3]. The evidence isn't just theoretical: in a study partly funded by NHLBI, smartphone use before bed was associated with shorter sleep than usual and worse sleep quality during the night [W-SRC-3]. The practical suggestion from experts is modest and specific — power devices down at least 30 minutes before getting into bed [W-SRC-3].

Daytime habits matter too. A nap can boost alertness and performance, and NHLBI's guidance treats napping as a legitimate tool rather than a failure of willpower [W-SRC-2]. The boundaries are worth knowing: adults should keep naps to no more than 20 minutes, and if falling asleep at night is a struggle, limiting naps or moving them earlier in the afternoon may help [W-SRC-2]. For preschool-age children, napping is normal and supports healthy growth and development — a reminder that sleep guidance is not one-size-fits-all [W-SRC-2].

Underneath all of it sits a scheduling question. Sleep is often the first thing busy people squeeze out of their days, and NHLBI's advice is to give yourself enough time to sleep in the first place — with enough of it, people may find they're happier and more productive during the day [W-SRC-2].

None of this is a diagnosis or a treatment plan. These are general habits drawn from public-health guidance, and individual sleep needs and circumstances vary. If sleep problems persist or worry you, that's a conversation for a clinician — NHLBI's own materials point readers toward professional evaluation for sleep disorders [W-SRC-1].

issues.title: The case for writing your sleep down
issues.dek: NHLBI's printable sleep diary turns vague tiredness into a pattern you can actually see — and, if you choose, bring to a doctor.
editorial: Most of us know roughly how much we slept last night. Far fewer of us can say how we slept this month, or what we drank, took, or scrolled on the nights we slept badly. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute offers a quietly practical answer: a printable sleep diary for recording the quality and quantity of your sleep, your use of medicines, alcohol, and caffeinated drinks, and how sleepy you feel during the day (W-SRC-5).

The value is in the columns you wouldn't think to track. Caffeine at 4 p.m., a glass of wine, a new medication — each lands in the same record as your bedtime and your morning grogginess, which is what makes patterns visible. NHLBI's suggestion is refreshingly low-tech: fill it in, then bring it with you to review with your doctor (W-SRC-5). It's a record, not a diagnosis.

It's also worth knowing that habits are only one branch of the map. NHLBI's treatment overview describes devices, therapies, medicines, and procedures for sleep disorders, with healthy sleep habits as the foundation and light therapy listed among the therapies (W-SRC-3). If your diary shows a stubborn pattern, that's information worth acting on — not a verdict.

One more distinction the institute draws that resists one-size-fits-all advice: there is a difference between the sleep you need to feel awake and the sleep you need to be healthy (W-SRC-4). Your diary is how you find your own line between the two. Individual sleep needs vary, and a week of honest notes will tell you more about yours than any general guideline.

issues.title: Game-Day Buffet, Zero Regrets
issues.dek: Party food lives by the clock, not by looks. The USDA's game-day guidance is really one rule wearing a jersey: keep hot food hot, cold food cold, and nothing lingering in between.
editorial: A buffet during a big game is a different animal from a sit-down dinner. Guests graze, platters sit out through a whole half, and the leftovers question arrives only after the final whistle. The USDA's guidance for exactly this scenario [P-SRC-4] boils down to watching two numbers: 40°F and 140°F.

Between those numbers lies what food-safety folks call the Danger Zone — the range where bacteria multiply quickly. Perishable food shouldn't sit in it for more than two hours, after which harmful bacteria can reach levels that make people sick [P-SRC-4]. If the room is above 90°F, that window shrinks to one hour [P-SRC-3].

The elegant fix is serving in batches. Put out one round of food for the first half and a fresh round later, keeping backup takeout refrigerated until it's needed, or hot at 140°F or above in a warming tray, slow cooker, or preheated oven. Cold dishes stay safe on ice at 40°F or below [P-SRC-4].

When the game ends, the clock keeps running. Refrigerate or freeze leftovers within two hours [P-SRC-4]. Cool big amounts fast by dividing them into shallow containers — a whole pot of soup cools too slowly and invites bacterial growth. Slice roasts, hams, and turkey breasts into smaller pieces; legs, wings, and thighs can stay whole [P-SRC-2].

Properly handled leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator or 3 to 4 months in the freezer, where they stay safe indefinitely but slowly lose moisture and flavor [P-SRC-2]. When reheating, bring food to 165°F — in the microwave, spread it evenly and cover it, then check the temperature with a food thermometer in several places [P-SRC-4]. Wrap or cover everything well; airtight storage keeps bacteria out, moisture in, and onion-chill odors where they belong [P-SRC-2].

editorial: Sleep hygiene isn't a certificate you earn once. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute frames it as something worth periodically taking stock of — the sleep environment you've built and the nighttime habits you've accumulated over the years [W-SRC-4]. The framing matters: what worked last season may have quietly stopped working.

The most common drift is luminous and pocket-sized. Artificial light from screens — phones, laptops, televisions — can signal the brain that it's time to be awake, and that exposure can translate into shorter sleep and irregular schedules in both children and adults [W-SRC-4]. In a study partly funded by NHLBI, smartphone use before bed was associated with shorter sleep duration than normal and worse sleep quality during the night [W-SRC-4].

For preschool-age children, napping is normal and promotes healthy growth and development [W-SRC-3]. Same behavior, different guidance, depending on who you are.

This is general public-health guidance, not individualized medical advice. NHLBI's sleep resources also cover recognizing sleep disorders such as insomnia and sleep apnea, avoiding dangerous drowsy driving, and coping with jet lag and nighttime shift work [W-SRC-2, W-SRC-1]. Persistent sleep concerns belong with a professional.

issues.title: The Leftover Ledger: A Calm Guide to What Keeps and What Goes
issues.dek: USDA guidance on leftovers is refreshingly unglamorous: cool fast, chill cold, reheat hot, and keep a running count. Here is the practical version for your kitchen.
editorial: Leftovers inspire two competing instincts: save everything forever, or quietly distrust anything older than yesterday. The USDA's guidance lands sensibly in between. Cooked leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, or 3 to 4 months in the freezer — after that, frozen food remains safe indefinitely but loses moisture and flavor [P-SRC-1].

The clock starts before the food reaches the fridge. Perishable foods — meat, poultry, eggs, casseroles, and restaurant take-home leftovers — should be discarded if left at room temperature longer than 2 hours, or 1 hour if the air temperature is above 90°F [P-SRC-3]. If takeout arrives early, hold it hot at 140°F or above, or keep cold dishes at 40°F or below on ice [P-SRC-4].

Cooling speed matters more than most cooks realize. A big pot of soup cools slowly, giving bacteria time to multiply; the fix is to divide large amounts into shallow containers and cut large items — roasts, hams, turkey — into smaller pieces before refrigerating. Turkey legs, wings, and thighs may be left whole [P-SRC-1].
When it's time to eat, reheat leftovers to 165°F. In the microwave, spread food evenly and cover it for even heating, and use a food thermometer to check the temperature in several places [P-SRC-4].

One honest limitation: this guidance tells you how long properly handled food keeps. It cannot tell you whether the container in the back of your fridge — with no record of when it was cooked or how it was stored — is safe. When storage history is unknown, the guidance is clear in spirit: foods stored longer may begin to spoil or become unsafe, and the advice is not to taste [P-SRC-3].
issues.pullquote: Refrigerate 3 to 4 days. Freeze 3 to 4 months. When the history is unknown, don't taste.

issues.dek: Local models are becoming first-class citizens in agent tooling — and the default network bindings of inference servers are the quiet security detail most builders skip.
editorial: The through-line across this week's packets is that wiring a local model into an agent stack has stopped being a hack. CSGLite positions itself as a lightweight local inference platform where a single command downloads a model, starts a server, and opens a chat session, with models staying loaded until you stop them manually and optional CSGHub access tokens for private models (M-SRC-1). QwenPaw makes the same bet from the assistant side: if you run local models — QwenPaw Local, Ollama, or LM Studio — no API keys or cloud services are required at all (M-SRC-5).

oh-my-pi shows how far the custom-provider pattern has spread: beyond built-in Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, and vLLM local backends, you can define any OpenAI-compatible endpoint in ~/.omp/agent/models.yml, specifying baseUrl, an apiKey placeholder, and per-model contextWindow and maxTokens values — their example configures MiniMax M3 with a 100000-token context window and 32000 max tokens (M-SRC-4).

The security note worth pinning above your desk: inference servers do not agree on a safe default bind address. Per the hermes-agent provider docs, Ollama, LM Studio, and llama-server all default to 127.0.0.1, while vLLM already binds to 0.0.0.0 — all interfaces — out of the box (M-SRC-2). If you flip a local server to 0.0.0.0 to reach it from another machine — OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 for Ollama, "Serve on Network" in LM Studio's Developer tab, or --host 0.0.0.0 for llama-server — you are exposing an unauthenticated inference endpoint to your network. Check what vLLM is already doing before you assume your setup is loopback-only.

One configuration detail that saves an afternoon: when hermes configures a custom endpoint via `hermes model`, it prompts for context length and auto-detects if you leave it blank — but their documented examples set it explicitly (qwen3.5:27b at 64000, deepseek-r1:70b at 65536). Manual setting is the fix when auto-detection gets a custom endpoint wrong (M-SRC-2).

issues.title: The Sleep Reset: Small Habits, Honest Variance
issues.dek: A federal sleep guide offers practical, non-judgmental steps for better rest — and a reminder that what 'enough' means varies from person to person.
editorial: Sleep is often the first thing busy people squeeze out of their schedules, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI). Their guidance reframes the trade: making time to sleep may help protect your health and well-being now and in the future, and with enough sleep each night you may find you're happier and more productive during the day. [W-SRC-2]

The mechanics matter here. NHLBI explains that internal body clocks running on roughly 24-hour cycles — regulated by light, darkness, and sleep schedules — govern when you're awake and when your body is ready for sleep. Once asleep, you cycle through sleep stages in a predictable pattern. [W-SRC-5]

One concrete, evidence-backed habit: power down devices. Artificial light from screens — phones, laptops, televisions — can signal the brain that it's time to be awake, and NHLBI-funded research has linked smartphone use before bed with shorter sleep duration and worse sleep quality. Experts cited by NHLBI suggest powering down at least 30 minutes before getting into bed. [W-SRC-3]

Naps get a nuanced treatment rather than a blanket rule. NHLBI notes that daytime napping may boost alertness and performance, but if you have trouble falling asleep at night, it may help to limit naps or take them earlier in the afternoon — and adults should nap for no more than 20 minutes. [W-SRC-2]

The honest caveat: individual sleep needs vary. NHLBI itself distinguishes between the sleep needed to feel awake and the sleep needed to be healthy. [W-SRC-4] This edition offers general guidance from a public-health source, not a diagnosis or a substitute for professional care — if you suspect a sleep disorder such as insomnia or sleep apnea, NHLBI's resources cover these conditions and point toward professional evaluation. [W-SRC-1]

issues.title: The Leftover Ledger: A Calm Guide to What Keeps and What Goes
issues.dek: USDA cold-storage windows, the two-hour rule, and a weekly fridge ritual — practical guidance for leftovers without guesswork.
editorial: Leftovers are one of the most common points of kitchen uncertainty: the container in the back of the fridge with no label and no story. The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service offers unusually clear, specific guidance here — not vague warnings, but actual day counts for cooked leftovers, raw meats, deli items, and more. This edition turns those numbers into a practical rhythm for your kitchen.

The core numbers are simple. Cooked leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator or 3 to 4 months in the freezer (P-SRC-2). Raw poultry and ground meats are shorter-lived: 1 to 2 days in the fridge (P-SRC-1). Deli salads, store-cooked entrees, and casseroles fall in the 3-to-5-day range (P-SRC-1). These are validity windows, not judgment calls — when the storage history is unknown, the guidance is to discard rather than guess.

The two-hour rule is the other anchor. Perishable food left at room temperature longer than 2 hours should be discarded — 1 hour if the room is above 90°F (P-SRC-3). Above 40°F and below 140°F is the 'Danger Zone' where bacteria multiply quickly (P-SRC-4). Reheat leftovers to 165°F, checking with a thermometer in several places (P-SRC-4).

Cooling matters as much as storage. Divide large batches — soup, roasts, turkey — into shallow containers or smaller pieces so food reaches 40°F or below quickly (P-SRC-2). Wrap well or use airtight containers to keep bacteria out and moisture in (P-SRC-2).

Finally, a weekly ritual: once a week, go through the fridge and discard perishables past their window (P-SRC-1). An open box of baking soda on a shelf keeps things smelling fresh (P-SRC-1). This is not alarmism — it is a small, repeatable habit that replaces uncertainty with a known answer.
issues.pullquote: Cooked leftovers: 3 to 4 days refrigerated, 3 to 4 months frozen. Raw poultry and ground meats: 1 to 2 days. When the clock is unknown, discard — don't guess.
